Even more important is the ratio of workers to funded or unfunded liabilities. Social security, for instance, started out with 12 workers to one drawee, now it's down to 4 to 1. There are something like 90 trillion dollars of health and social entitlements that are lacking future funding. On top of that the total, available number of hours to work, not jobs, is shrinking, which is causing the executive branch to take steps to cut the number of hours American workers work, so as to better spread those hours out. Thus the new 30 hours a week full time, and the new $51,000 salaried over time decision.

Greece's retirement age is 52. When Social Security was set up here in the United States, the draw age was 65, but the average life span was 62 so most people didn't even get to take any, So, originally, there were 12 people paying for every retiree, now there are only 4 to 1 and by 2030 (only 14 years away) there will only be 2 people paying the retirement benefits (Social Security and Medicare) for every one retiree. Not only these federal level unfunded liabilities (one out-there estimate at $209 TRILLION dollars!), there is a state and county level financial time bomb, pensions. The states, in the sixties, traded higher wages for their employees with a guarantee that the state will give them a great retirement pension. So, you work 30 years for the State of California, the State of California will pay you 80% of your HIGHEST yearly salary every year, for the rest of your life. Retire at 65, work as a secretary at $45,000 per year, you get $36,000 a year, for the rest of your life. If you live in California, you also have your healthcare taken care of for the rest of your life. This is also encoded into the California State Constitution, the first dollars in taxes taken in are used to pay the pensions, then everything else in the state such as roads and schools get paid. Times that by 100's of thousands of retirees and you have a pension deficit of 52%. And California is one of the better states. Every state in the Union has billions of dollars that they are going to have to come up with to pay their employee's pensions. That's why you are currently seeing states, cities, and counties trying tricks to get out from under the pension burdens like bankruptcy (Stockton CA, Detroit MI) and state's breaking unions (Wisconsin). But all in all, it's tick-tock the clock counting down to the time when the current and future generation is going to turn off the entitlement spigot, whether by choice or circumstance and leave millions of senior citizens to freeze to death, homeless and broke.
